blocks.text: Support and movement are fundamental aspects of human biology, enabling us to perform a wide range of activities from basic locomotion to complex tasks. Bones, cartilage and other connective tissues make an internal framework, the skeleton, that provides structural support, protects vital organs, and produces movement and locomotion.
Structure of bone

Bones are made of connective tissue reinforced with calcium and specialised bone cells. The surface of a bone is covered by a tough membrane, the periosteum. The thick layer under the periosteum is made of hard material, compact bone, which makes up the majority of the bone tissue. The broad ends of a bone are the epiphyses, and the middle part along its length is the diaphysis or shaft.

The basic structural units of compact bone are the Haversian systems. A Haversian system is made of lamellae, concentric layers of mineralised extracellular matrix containing collagen fibres and small needle-shaped crystals of calcium phosphate; the crystals are brittle but rigid, giving bone great strength, while collagen is flexible but weak, so bone is both strong and flexible. The lamellae are separated by small spaces, the lacunae, in which the osteocytes, the mature bone cells, are located; the osteocytes are connected to each other and to the Haversian canal by small channels, the canaliculi. The concentric lamellae surround a central Haversian canal, which contains blood vessels, nerves and lymphatic vessels. Small channels running perpendicular to the Haversian canals connect them with each other and with the periosteum and also carry blood vessels, nerves and lymphatic vessels, and collagen fibres anchor the periosteum to the underlying bone, giving additional strength and stability. Beneath the compact bone is spongy bone, a latticework of bony spikes that makes it light and strong.
Bone marrow

Many bones also contain a soft tissue, bone marrow, which can be red or yellow. Red bone marrow is found in spongy bone, the ends of long bones, the ribs, vertebrae, sternum and pelvis, and produces red blood cells, platelets and white blood cells. Yellow bone marrow fills the shafts of long bones; it consists mostly of fat cells and serves as an energy reserve, and it can be converted to red marrow to produce blood cells when severe blood loss occurs.

blocks.title: Living bone
blocks.text: Despite their number and size, bones make up less than 20% of the body's mass. Bones are not the dry, rigid structures they appear to be; they are moist, living tissues.
Types of bone cells

Three types of cell, osteoblasts, osteocytes and osteoclasts, are involved in the development, growth and remodelling of bones. Osteoblasts are bone-forming cells that synthesise and secrete the unmineralised ground substance; once surrounded by matrix they become osteocytes. Osteocytes are mature bone cells that maintain healthy bone tissue by secreting enzymes and bone mineral content, and regulate the release of calcium from bone to blood. Osteoclasts develop from macrophages and carry out bone resorption: they break down bone and release calcium and phosphate into the blood, work that is important to the growth and repair of bone.
Bone development

The process of bone formation is osteogenesis. It begins during embryonic development and continues throughout life, playing a vital role in the growth, maintenance and repair of bones. There are two primary pathways.

items: Long bones such as the femur and humerus form by the transition of cartilage into bone. The centre of the cartilage begins to harden (calcify), the chondrocytes (cartilage cells) there die and leave cavities, and blood vessels penetrate the cavities and bring osteoblasts and osteoclasts. The osteoblasts start building bone tissue, replacing the cartilage with new bone; the step by which cartilage is replaced by bone through the deposition of minerals is ossification. The osteoclasts break down the calcified cartilage, making room for more bone to form. As the bone matures some osteoblasts become trapped within the bone tissue and transform into osteocytes, which maintain the bone structure. The process continues until all the cartilage is changed to bone except the cartilage that remains at the articular (joint) surfaces.

A few bones, for example some bones of the skull, develop directly into hard bone without forming cartilage first. Their osteocytes are at first scattered randomly through the embryonic connective tissue but soon fuse into layers and become flat plates of bone.

blocks.title: Remodelling
blocks.text: Even after the bones have fully formed, osteogenesis continues as bone remodelling, the ongoing breakdown of old bone by osteoclasts and formation of new bone by osteoblasts.

blocks.long_description: A long bone has broad epiphyses of spongy bone holding red marrow and a diaphysis of compact bone under the periosteum around a cavity of yellow marrow. Compact bone is built of Haversian systems: concentric lamellae of collagen and calcium phosphate around a Haversian canal carrying vessels and nerves, with osteocytes in lacunae linked by canaliculi. Osteoblasts lay down matrix and become osteocytes, which maintain the bone and regulate calcium; osteoclasts, from macrophages, resorb bone. In ossification a cartilage model calcifies, its chondrocytes die, vessels bring in osteoblasts and osteoclasts, and bone replaces the cartilage except at the joint surfaces; some skull bones form directly as flat plates.

blocks.text: Structure of cartilage

Most of the cartilage of the foetus is replaced by bone, but some remains throughout life and provides flexibility, for example between bones, at the end of the nose, in the outer ear and along the inside of the trachea. A layer of connective tissue, the perichondrium, surrounds the cartilage and contains the blood vessels, lymphatic vessels and nerves that supply it. Inside the perichondrium is the cartilage matrix, composed of collagen, elastin, proteoglycans and other fibres, which gives the tissue its strength, flexibility and resistance to compression. Unlike other connective tissues, there are no blood vessels inside the cartilage matrix; the cells are supplied by diffusion, and because of this cartilage heals very slowly. The cartilage cells, the chondrocytes, lie within small spaces, lacunae, embedded in the matrix, and are responsible for synthesising and maintaining it.
Cartilage types

Cartilage is of three types. Hyaline cartilage is the most common and is found in the nose, trachea and the articulating surfaces of bones in joints. Fibrocartilage is found where the body experiences high stress and tension, such as the intervertebral discs and the pubic symphysis. Elastic cartilage is found in the external ear and the epiglottis.

blocks.alt: Three panels of cartilage: hyaline with oval chondrocytes in a plain blue matrix, fibrocartilage with chondrocytes between wavy collagen bundles, and elastic cartilage with chondrocytes among zigzag elastic fibres. A box below lists what all cartilage shares.
blocks.caption: The three types of cartilage and the structure they share (original diagram after Figure 12.4).
blocks.long_description: Every cartilage is wrapped in a perichondrium carrying vessels and nerves, and inside has a matrix of collagen, elastin, proteoglycans and other fibres with no blood vessels, so its chondrocytes, sitting in lacunae, are fed by diffusion and it heals slowly. Hyaline cartilage, the commonest, has a glassy matrix and lines the nose, trachea and joint surfaces; fibrocartilage is packed with collagen bundles for the stress of the intervertebral discs and pubic symphysis; elastic cartilage has elastic fibres that let the external ear and epiglottis spring back.

blocks.text: Arrangement of bones in the skeleton
The human skeletal system consists of 206 bones, in two main divisions: the axial skeleton and the appendicular skeleton.
Axial skeleton
The axial skeleton forms the axis of the body; its bones support and protect the organs of the head, neck and chest. It consists of the skull, ribs, spine and sternum.

items: Skull: 22 bones. Eight cranial bones form the cranium (brain box): the two paired bones are the parietal and temporal bones, and the four unpaired bones are the frontal, occipital, ethmoid and sphenoid. Fourteen facial bones are attached to the cranium: the six paired bones are the lacrimal, zygomatic, nasal, inferior nasal concha, maxilla and palatine, and the two unpaired bones are the mandible (jaw bone) and vomer.
Middle ear: six bones (three pairs), the ossicles: malleus, incus and stapes.
Neck bone: the hyoid is a small single bone at the base of the skull below the tongue; it does not articulate with any other bone of the head.

Vertebral column: 33 vertebrae in five groups. Seven cervical vertebrae in the neck, the first called the atlas and the second the axis; twelve thoracic vertebrae in the chest, which carry the ribs; five lumbar vertebrae in the abdominal region; five sacral vertebrae fused into the sacrum, which articulates with the iliac bones of the hip to form the back of the pelvis; and four coccygeal vertebrae or coccyx, fused in adults. The sacral and coccygeal vertebrae together are the pelvic vertebrae.

Rib cage and chest bone: 24 ribs (12 pairs) and a sternum, the long flat chest bone in the centre of the chest. The ribs articulate behind with the thoracic vertebrae; in front, seven pairs attach directly to the sternum by separate costal cartilages (true ribs), the 8th, 9th and 10th pairs attach by a common costal cartilage (false ribs), and the last two pairs (11th and 12th) are floating ribs that do not attach to the sternum.

blocks.text: Appendicular skeleton
The appendicular skeleton includes the bones of the appendages, the arms and legs: the pectoral girdle, pelvic girdle, forelimbs and hindlimbs.

items: Pectoral girdle: two pairs of bones, a pair of clavicles (collar bones) and a pair of scapulae (shoulder bones). One end of each clavicle articulates with the sternum and the other with the scapula.

Forelimbs: each arm, wrist, hand and fingers has 30 bones. One humerus, a long bone whose spherical head fits into the glenoid cavity; one ulna and one radius, long bones, the ulna on the inner side of the arm and the radius on the outer (thumb) side, the ulna slightly bigger; eight carpals, short bones in two rows forming the wrist, the upper row articulating with the radius at the wrist joint; five metacarpals making the palm; and fourteen phalanges, three in each finger and two in the thumb.

Pelvic girdle: two hip bones, each of three bones, the ilium, ischium and pubis, whose fusion forms a bony socket, the acetabulum. The two hip bones are joined at the front by the pubic symphysis, a cartilaginous joint at the midline of the body.

Hindlimbs: each leg, ankle, foot and toes has 30 bones. One femur, the long thigh bone whose head fits into the acetabulum; one patella or kneecap, embedded in the long tendon that runs over the knee joint; one tibia or shin bone, the large bone of the leg, and one fibula, the thin outer bone that joins the tibia just below the knee and just above the ankle; seven tarsals, short bones tightly attached to form the ankle; five metatarsals, articulating with the tarsals and phalanges to form the sole; and fourteen phalanges, three in each toe and two in the big toe.

blocks.alt: A stick-figure skeleton with the axial bones in blue (skull, spine, ribs and sternum) and the appendicular bones in orange (pectoral girdle and arms, pelvis and legs). Labels on the left list the skull, vertebral groups and rib cage; labels on the right list the girdles and the 30 bones of each limb.
blocks.caption: The 206 bones of the skeleton: axial in blue, appendicular in orange (original schematic after Figures 12.5 to 12.9).
blocks.long_description: The axial skeleton is the skull of 22 bones (8 cranial, 14 facial) with 6 ear ossicles and the hyoid, the vertebral column of 33 vertebrae (7 cervical including atlas and axis, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 4 coccygeal) and the rib cage of 12 pairs of ribs (7 true, 3 false, 2 floating) with the sternum. The appendicular skeleton is the pectoral girdle (2 clavicles, 2 scapulae), each forelimb of 30 bones (humerus, ulna, radius, 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges), the pelvic girdle (two hip bones of ilium, ischium and pubis meeting at the acetabulum and joined at the pubic symphysis) and each hindlimb of 30 bones (femur, patella, tibia, fibula, 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges).

blocks.text: Joints

A joint is a place where two bones, or a bone and cartilage, come together. Three major kinds are found in the human body: fibrous (immovable) joints, cartilaginous (slightly movable) joints and synovial (freely movable) joints.

items: Fibrous joints: the bones are directly connected by fibrous connective tissue consisting mainly of collagen, and no movement is permitted. Examples are the sutures between the immovable bones of the skull, the joints between the tibia and fibula in the lower leg, and the joints between the teeth and their sockets in the jawbone.

Cartilaginous joints: the bones are connected by a layer of cartilage and little movement is allowed. In some the bones are connected by hyaline cartilage, for example the joint between the first rib and the sternum; in others by fibrocartilage, for example the pubic symphysis of the pelvic girdle and the intervertebral discs.

Synovial joints: the most common type, allowing a wide range of movement. A smooth, tough, elastic hyaline cartilage, the articular cartilage, covers the ends of the bones and provides a smooth, frictionless surface. A fibrous capsule surrounds the joint and helps to hold the bones together; it has an outer layer of ligaments and an inner lining of synovial membrane, which secretes the synovial fluid that lubricates the joint. The strong bands of connective tissue that connect the bones are the ligaments.

blocks.text: There are six main types of synovial joint, by their range of motion. Ball-and-socket joints allow motion in all directions, as at the shoulder and hip. Hinge joints allow movement in only one plane, like a door hinge, as at the elbow and knee. Pivot joints allow rotation around a single axis, as between the first and second vertebrae of the neck. Ellipsoidal joints allow movement in two planes but not rotation, as at the wrist with the radius. Saddle joints allow movement in two planes because one bone has a concave surface and the other a convex one, as at the thumb. Gliding joints allow gliding movements between bones, as between the vertebrae and between the bones of the wrist and ankle.

blocks.alt: Left: a fibrous joint with a zigzag collagen seam and a cartilaginous joint with a blue cartilage pad between two bones. Right: a synovial joint in section with blue articular cartilage on each bone end, a green synovial cavity and a brown capsule, labelled. A box lists the six kinds of synovial joint and joint transplantation.
blocks.caption: Fibrous, cartilaginous and synovial joints, and the structure of a synovial joint (original diagram after Figure 12.10).
blocks.long_description: In a fibrous joint collagen binds the bones so they cannot move, as in the skull sutures. In a cartilaginous joint a pad of hyaline cartilage or fibrocartilage allows slight movement, as at the first rib and the intervertebral discs. In a synovial joint the bone ends are capped by articular cartilage, a fibrous capsule of ligaments holds them together, and its synovial membrane secretes the fluid that lubricates the cavity, allowing free movement: ball-and-socket, hinge, pivot, ellipsoidal, saddle and gliding joints differ in their range. Damaged joints can be replaced wholly or partly by artificial parts, by a donor joint, or by implanted chondrocytes.

blocks.title: Joint transplantation
blocks.text: Joint transplantation is a surgical procedure in which a damaged joint is replaced with a healthy natural joint from a donor or an artificial joint. In total joint replacement the entire damaged joint is replaced with an artificial joint of metal, plastic or ceramic; in partial joint replacement only the damaged part is replaced with an artificial component, often in the knee; in allograft transplantation a healthy joint from a donor replaces the damaged joint, often in the ankle and knee; and in chondrocyte implantation chondrocytes from the patient's own joint are implanted into the damaged joint, often in the knee.
Skeleton, musculature and bipedal posture

The bipedal posture of humans is linked to the skeleton and musculature in several ways. The human vertebral column has a distinctive S-shaped curve, which distributes weight evenly and maintains balance while standing and walking. The pelvis is shorter and broader, which stabilises the torso and supports the body's weight on two legs. The femur is angled inward towards the knee, keeping the body's centre of mass over the feet for stability while standing and walking. The muscles of the buttocks are much larger in humans and stabilise the torso and propel the body forward while walking, and the calf muscles are well developed, providing power for walking and running. The foot has a longitudinal arch that absorbs shock and distributes weight evenly, and the toes are shorter and less prehensile, so the foot works more effectively as a lever during walking and running.

blocks.title: Problems due to improper posture
blocks.text: Improper posture can harm bones and joints. Vertebral misalignment can lead to back and neck pain and herniated discs by putting pressure on the vertebrae and nerves. Joint strain in the neck, shoulders, hips and knees leads to pain, inflammation and potentially arthritis. Muscle imbalances, from muscles overused and underused by poor posture, can pull bones and joints out of alignment.

blocks.prompt: A fractured femur heals in a few months, but a torn piece of articular cartilage in the knee may never fully repair. Explain the difference from the structure of the two tissues.
blocks.explanation: Bone has blood vessels in its Haversian canals and periosteum, and living osteoblasts, osteocytes and osteoclasts that remodel it throughout life, so it can grow and repair itself. Cartilage matrix has no blood vessels; its chondrocytes in their lacunae are fed only by diffusion through the matrix, so it has limited ability to repair itself and heals very slowly.

blocks.text: Quick recap

items: Bone: periosteum over compact bone (Haversian systems of lamellae, lacunae with osteocytes, canaliculi, a central canal) over spongy bone; red marrow makes blood cells, yellow marrow stores fat; epiphyses and diaphysis.
Osteoblasts build, osteocytes maintain, osteoclasts resorb. Long bones ossify from a cartilage model; some skull bones form directly; remodelling continues all life.

Cartilage: perichondrium, avascular matrix of collagen, elastin and proteoglycans, chondrocytes in lacunae; hyaline (nose, trachea, joints), fibrocartilage (discs, pubic symphysis), elastic (ear, epiglottis); slow to heal.
206 bones: axial (skull 22, ossicles 6, hyoid, 33 vertebrae in five groups, 24 ribs and sternum) and appendicular (pectoral girdle, 30-bone forelimbs, pelvic girdle, 30-bone hindlimbs).

Joints: fibrous (immovable), cartilaginous (slightly movable), synovial (free; articular cartilage, capsule, ligaments, synovial fluid; six types). Bipedal posture rests on the S-shaped spine, broad pelvis, angled femur, buttock and calf muscles, arched foot and short toes.
